cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal:
Work over the complex field \(\mathbb C\). Is the following general cubic formulation of the asymptotic rank conjecture true?
\[\forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall T\in\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n:\quad \bigl(\operatorname{rank}F_1(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_2(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_3(T)=n\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \widetilde R(T)=n,\]
where \(F_i(T)\) are the three matrix flattenings and
\[\widetilde R(T)=\lim_{k\to\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\inf_{k\ge1}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}?\]
Here \(R\) is exact tensor rank, and \(\boxtimes\) groups corresponding factors of tensor products. The tensor \(T\) and its dimension \(n\) are fixed while \(k\) tends to infinity. The quantifier covers all complex tensors satisfying the flattening condition; no additional symmetry, support or computational promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
Tensors and flattenings. For a positive integer \(d\), let \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb C^d\). A tensor \(T\) in three factors of dimensions \(a,b,c\) is the coefficient array \((t_{ij\ell})_{(i,j,\ell)\in[a]\times[b]\times[c]}\), interpreted as \(\sum_{i,j,\ell}t_{ij\ell}e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_\ell\). For the cubic format \(a=b=c=n\), define three \(n\)-by-\(n^2\) matrices by
\[(F_1(T))_{i,(j,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_2(T))_{j,(i,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_3(T))_{\ell,(i,j)}=t_{ij\ell}.\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically; the ordering does not affect matrix rank. Matrix rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb C\). A tensor is concise in this format when all three matrix ranks are \(n\). This excludes zero tensors and tensors that effectively use a smaller subspace in some factor. For \(n=1\), it just means a nonzero scalar.

Exact rank. For any positive dimensions \(a,b,c\), define
\[R(S)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N:\ S=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s,\quad u_s\in\mathbb C^a,\ v_s\in\mathbb C^b,\ w_s\in\mathbb C^c\right\}.\]
The empty sum is zero. A pure tensor has coefficients \((u_i v_j w_\ell)\); equality in a decomposition is exact coefficientwise equality. Finite decompositions always exist, so the minimum is well-defined. The three vectors in a summand are independent choices: there is no symmetric-rank restriction. Their complex entries are unrestricted, including noncomputable numbers; the question does not ask for a finite input encoding or an algorithm to find the decomposition.

Grouped powers. For \(k\ge1\), the tensor \(T^{\boxtimes k}\) has exactly three factors, each with coordinates indexed by \([n]^k\), and hence each of dimension \(n^k\). Its entries are
\[(T^{\boxtimes k})_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k),(j_1,\ldots,j_k),(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)}=\prod_{h=1}^{k}t_{i_h j_h\ell_h}.\]
Its rank is taken after this grouping. A vector in a rank decomposition may be any element of \(\mathbb C^{n^k}\); it need not itself split into \(k\) vectors of dimension \(n\). Thus ranks of grouped powers need not equal \(R(T)^k\).

Asymptotic value. Tensoring decompositions gives
\[R(T^{\boxtimes(k+\ell)})\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})R(T^{\boxtimes\ell}).\]
For a concise tensor the elementary flattening lower bound and a slice decomposition give
\[n^k\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le n^{2k}.\]
Subadditivity of the logarithms therefore proves existence of the positive real limit in the question and its equality with the displayed infimum. In particular \(n\le\widetilde R(T)\le n^2\). The proposed equality is equivalently
\[\forall n\ \forall T\text{ concise}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists K\ge1\ \forall k\ge K:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le(n+\varepsilon)^k.\]
Here \(K\) may depend on \(n,T,\varepsilon\), with no uniform or effective rate required. The actual decompositions may depend on \(k\) as well. Neither attainment of the infimum at a finite power nor rank \(n^k\) for any finite power is asserted.

Related ranks. Border rank of \(S\) is the least integer \(r\) such that \(S\) is a Euclidean limit of tensors of exact rank at most \(r\) in its fixed complex coefficient space. The defining ranks in this card are exact ranks. A finite-power border-rank result or a finite-power exact-rank lower bound must be connected to the quantified asymptotic statement before it can settle this question.

context_blocks.text: A rank decomposition expresses a three-factor tensor as a sum of elementary products. Allowing many copies to be processed jointly can save products because vectors in each grouped factor can correlate different copies. The conjecture says that these savings eventually leave no exponential overhead above the flattening lower bound. For the diagonal tensor \(\Delta_n=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\), the elementary decomposition and flattening bound already match at every power.

The matrix multiplication tensor \(M_m=\sum_{i,j,\ell=1}^{m}e_{ij}\otimes e_{j\ell}\otimes e_{\ell i}\) is concise in three factors of dimension \(m^2\). In particular \(\widetilde R(M_2)=2^\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum of exponents for arithmetic matrix multiplication over \(\mathbb C\). The proposed equality for this tensor would give \(\omega=2\). The implication in the reverse direction is not known from this example; the card quantifies over far more than matrix multiplication tensors.

The literature uses both general and restricted formulations. The retained target is the general cubic concise formulation discussed in the primary source and in the April 2026 spectrum paper. Lee’s January 2026 Conjecture 1 additionally assumes tightness: after suitable basis choices, injective integer weights on each factor sum to zero on every nonzero coefficient. That extra support condition is absent here. The numerical census supplies data for upper bounds, not a proof of this universal equality.

The June 2026 revision of the primary paper proves that each asymptotic-rank sublevel set is defined by vanishing of finitely many polynomials, and that a nonincreasing sequence of attainable asymptotic ranks eventually stabilizes. Its threshold-decision theorem applies over computable fields and is nonuniform in the threshold. These structural results do not identify all values with the flattening bound or supply an effective solution for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Alman, Li and Pratt’s April 2026 paper characterizes one part of the asymptotic tensor spectrum and gives algorithms for its edge support functionals. The spectrum is a collection of normalized, additive, multiplicative and restriction-monotone tensor parameters; its full maximum describes asymptotic rank. Characterizing selected members does not prove that they exhaust the spectrum. The paper explicitly separates its edge results from the full rank conjecture.

Two September 2026 papers give new lower bounds for individual tensors. Yang treats exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication; Mańdziuk determines border ranks for specified direct sums and products. Neither inspected theorem supplies a single concise cubic tensor with a positive asymptotic gap above its dimension. Such finite-tensor lower bounds are compatible with the conjecture.

Holtrup and Zuiddam’s 15 September 2026 preprint settles a different extremal question: it bounds and classifies the largest stabilizer dimension of concise cubic tensors. A stabilizer consists of invertible changes of basis that preserve the tensor. Maximizing that group dimension does not determine the rank growth of all tensor powers, so this new result is not a resolution of the card.

cards.why: The conjecture asks whether every bilinear operation attains, in the exponential growth rate of jointly processed copies, the elementary lower bound already visible from matrices. A positive answer would force matrix multiplication exponent two and impose a simple common asymptotic law on all concise tensors. A negative answer would exhibit an obstruction that survives arbitrarily many grouped copies, beyond the familiar difficulty of decomposing a single tensor.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation, including the stated limit convention. An affirmative proof must cover every positive dimension and every concise complex tensor, with arbitrarily small positive \(\varepsilon\) in the equivalent power bound. A negative proof must establish the existence of a positive integer \(n\), a concise \(T\) in the specified cubic format, and a real \(\eta>0\) such that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\ge(n+\eta)^k.\]
This is equivalent to a counterexample with \(\widetilde R(T)>n\); no explicitness or computability condition is added to the counterexample. A large rank at one power is insufficient. A result only for a restricted class of tensors, only over another field, or conditional on an unproved complexity assumption does not settle the universal complex-field target. This is an exact yes/no conjecture, so a fixed additive tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the equality.

progress.text: The original primary preprint establishes structural results for asymptotic tensor rank; its June 2026 revision gives the current statements used here.
Lee reports a numerical census improving upper-bound data in five computationally accessible formats and states the tight concise conjecture. The experiments do not certify the unrestricted equality.
Alman, Li and Pratt establish edge support functionals over arbitrary fields and characterize them using matrix multiplication. Their result does not characterize the full spectrum.
The revised primary source gives Zariski-closed sublevel sets, threshold-specific decision algorithms over computable fields and discreteness from above, while retaining the rank conjecture.
Mańdziuk gives new border-rank lower bounds for specific direct sums and products; the checked results do not provide an asymptotic counterexample.
Yang proves lower bounds for exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication. The power-uniform exponential gap required here is a different guarantee.
Holtrup and Zuiddam determine the maximum stabilizer dimension for all concise cubic tensors, resolving that separate symmetry question.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The general cubic concise equality over C remains open in the inspected primary sources. The June structural characterization and April edge-spectrum results do not prove it. The checked September exact-rank, border-rank and stabilizer-dimension theorems address different guarantees, and the January numerical census is not a universal proof. This is a bounded source review, not a certification that no resolution exists.

Some sources, including Lee’s Conjecture 1, state a version restricted to tight concise tensors. That additional hypothesis has not been silently added to the selected target.

sentences: A three-factor tensor can be decomposed into elementary products, and its rank is the least number of those products.
The question asks whether every concise complex tensor of equal factor dimension has asymptotic rank exactly that dimension when corresponding factors of many copies are grouped.
The dimension and tensor stay fixed during the limit, and no tightness, symmetry, computability or uniform convergence promise is imposed.
A complete Lean proof must establish the equality for all such tensors or a counterexample whose grouped powers all require a strictly larger exponential base.
The inspected 2026 structural, numerical, finite-rank and symmetry results do not settle this general asymptotic equality.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
